exp.0:1:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, weeps bitterly through the night, and her tears run down her face. No one comforts her. The "lovers" are the allies and nations that once seemed to support her. The phrase about her friends means they betrayed her and even became her enemies.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so. The speaker is the poet, who describes the city as a helpless widow. The grief is deep because the allies she trusted did not help her.

Today it reminds us that God is not alarmed by our tears, and that the Bible makes room for sincere weeping. If someone failed you in your pain, do not keep it silent: bring it to God in prayer and seek faithful people who will walk alongside you.
exp.0:12:
It says that God sent fire from above into the depths of the person, and that this pain overpowered her. He also spread a net to catch her feet and turned her back. The phrase that the fire took control means that the fire gained mastery over her. "Desolate" means destroyed and left empty. In the end, she is left with a pain that seems never to end.

The speaker is Jerusalem, pictured as a woman weeping after the fall of the city, probably before the Babylonians. The book is usually attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. She understands her suffering as the consequence of God's judgment for her rebellions, as the next verse shows. These are poetic images, not a literal description.

For today: when pain overwhelms us, we can speak about it with God honestly, without pretending to be strong. Lamentations teaches us that weeping before Him is also a form of faith.
exp.0:13:
Jerusalem describes her own sins as a yoke, a heavy wooden frame fastened around the neck of an animal. Those rebellions are twisted together and now press down on her neck, the back of her neck. Her strength has failed. The Lord has handed her over to enemies she can no longer withstand.

The one speaking is the city of Jerusalem, portrayed as a suffering woman. Lamentations is a song of mourning over the fall of the city, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. The poem acknowledges that this ruin is connected to the people's rebellion, so the grief is mixed with confession.

For today: when you carry the consequences of your own mistakes, do not hide them or sink into despair. Acknowledge them honestly before God, asking for his forgiveness and his help to get back on your feet.
exp.0:14:
He says that the Lord trampled all the brave men of Jerusalem who were within her. He also called together a force, an army, to destroy the young men. To trample is to tread down, and the young men are the youths. Judah, called the virgin daughter, was trodden down by the Lord the way grapes are trodden in the winepress, where the juice is squeezed out.

The one speaking is the city of Jerusalem, pictured as a suffering woman. Lamentations mourns the fall of the city, which many connect with the Babylonian conquest of 586 B.C. The poem acknowledges that this came because of the people's rebellions, and it describes it with very harsh images.

For today: we can bring our pain to God honestly, without covering it up. This book teaches us to lament and to recognize our failings, without losing hope that God remains our refuge.
exp.0:15:
He says the one speaking weeps without stopping. His eyes run with water, meaning the tears flow like a river. He weeps because the comforter has gone far from him, someone who would bring rest or relief to his soul. His children are ruined and lost because the enemy has won and overcome them.

The one speaking is Jerusalem, pictured as a suffering woman, though the book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah (the tradition says so, but the text does not give his name). After the city fell to Babylon, the people are in ruins and in captivity. She acknowledges that her own rebellions had a part in this pain.

For today: when you are hurt, do not hide your weeping. Bring it honestly to God and also seek out people who can walk with you. Crying is not a lack of faith; it is an honest way to ask for comfort.
exp.0:18:
It says that Jerusalem called for help from her "lovers," that is, the allies she trusted, but they betrayed her. It also says that her priests and elders, the leaders of the people, died inside the city while they were searching for food to keep themselves alive. To keep her life going a little longer means to keep it sustained for a while longer.

The speaker is the city of Jerusalem, personified as a weeping woman, after the destruction by Babylon. She acknowledges that the LORD is righteous and that she rebelled against him. Many understand the "lovers" as allied nations or false gods; the text does not make this entirely clear. The hunger of the siege left everyone weakened, even the leaders.

For today: when human securities fail us, we can stop seeking support in what does not sustain us and turn back to God with sincerity, acknowledging our faults and asking him for comfort.
exp.0:19:
Here Jerusalem asks God to look at her distress. She says her bowels are troubled, meaning she feels a deep pain, like a knot in the stomach, and that her heart is turned within her, stirred up inside. She acknowledges that she has grievously rebelled. Abroad the sword bereaves, which means the sword leaves mothers without children. And at home there is as death: hunger, sickness, and mourning.

The city of Jerusalem speaks, personified as a grieving woman, after being destroyed and after her people were taken into exile. Many understand that the book was written by Jeremiah, though the text does not say so directly. She recognizes that God is righteous and that her suffering is tied to her sin.

For today: when you suffer or have failed, do not hide from God. Bring Him your pain and your guilt with sincerity, trusting that He listens.
exp.1:0:
This verse is a lament. It says that God, in his anger, covered Jerusalem, called here the daughter of Zion, with darkness. The glory of Israel was thrown from heaven down to the earth, meaning it lost its honor and its height. The footstool of his feet is usually understood as the temple or the ark, the place where God was felt to be present.

Lamentations is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not name its author. The poet mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 BC. He interprets that ruin as the consequence of God's judgment for the people's sin, and he expresses it with grief and amazement.

For today: when we go through losses or painful consequences, we can weep honestly before God, without pretending. And even in the midst of pain, we can acknowledge our mistakes and return to him, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:4:
God acted against Israel as if he were an enemy. He allowed her palaces and her strongholds to fall, and so the grief grew among the people of Judah. "Daughter of Judah" is a poetic way of speaking about the people of Judah. "Swallowed up" means that he utterly destroyed or tore down. "Mourning and lamentation" means weeping and complaint over a great loss.

Lamentations is a song of sorrow over the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. The poet sees the destruction as the consequence of God's judgment for the sin of the people. He speaks with pain and with honesty.

For today: when you suffer and do not understand why, you can bring your pain before God without disguises. Lamenting before him is a form of faith, because you keep coming to him.
exp.1:8:
This verse describes the fall of Jerusalem. Its gates have sunk into the ground, and the bars that protected the city have been broken. The king and the princes are carried off into exile among the nations, where there is no law, meaning there is no knowledge of God's law. The prophets also receive no vision from the Lord: God is silent.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations. A tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the book itself does not say so. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, and he understands that judgment as the work of God because of the people's sin. The poem describes the ruin of the city, of its worship, and of its leadership.

For today: when you feel that everything is collapsing and God seems silent, do not pretend to be strong. Follow this lament: bring your pain honestly to him and keep seeking him, trusting that his silence is not his final word.
exp.1:9:
The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground and say nothing. They throw dust on their heads and dress in sackcloth, a rough cloth used to show deep sorrow. The young women, who once had joy, bow their heads to the ground. "Daughter of Zion" is a poetic way of naming the city and its people.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He looks at the ruin of Jerusalem, probably the fall of 586 BC, and understands it as God's judgment for the people's sin. He describes the grief of everyone, from the elders to the young women.

For today: when the pain is so great that you have no words, you can be silent and weep before God. He does not ask you to pretend to be strong, but to come near to him with honesty.
exp.1:11:
Small children, hungry, were asking their mothers for bread and wine, but there was nothing left. They fainted in the streets like wounded soldiers, and at the end they died in their mothers' arms. The phrase about their lives being poured out is not explained further here, so the sense of their life slipping away little by little is simply carried in the verse itself.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after it was besieged and destroyed by Babylon. The hunger was terrible, and the writer laments that the false prophets did not speak the truth about the sin of the people.

Today we can learn not to ignore the pain of children who go hungry or lack what they need. God grieves with those who suffer, and invites us to weep with them and to help in concrete ways: sharing food, supporting a family, or serving at a community kitchen.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that the people passing by Jerusalem mocked her. "Clap their hands" was clapping or striking the palms as a sign of scorn, and "hiss" and wagging the head expressed contempt. They asked, "Is this the city that men call the perfection of beauty, the joy of the whole earth?"

The one speaking is the poet of Lamentations, who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. Many think it was Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. The text explains that the fall came because of the sin of the people and because of prophets who gave false hope instead of warning. The neighbors, far from offering comfort, mocked.

For today: when you see someone fall, do not mock or rejoice. Offer them compassion and, if needed, an honest word spoken in love.
exp.1:18:
It says that someone should rise up in the dead of night and cry out to God with complete sincerity. Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord would have been the picture of telling God everything we feel without holding anything back. Lifting up the hands was a gesture of prayer and pleading. Help is asked above all for the children, who faint from hunger at the corners of the streets.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this clearly. The speaker describes the pain of the destroyed city and encourages Jerusalem not to stay silent, but to bring its anguish to God, even in the middle of judgment.

When sorrow overwhelms us, we do not have to pretend to be strong. We can pray honestly, weep before God, and intercede for those who suffer most near us, such as children and the vulnerable.
exp.2:0:
It says that someone has gone through a very great suffering. The "rod" was the stick a shepherd or a father used to correct, and here it stands for God's punishment. His "wrath" is his anger. The speaker feels that God himself is striking him.

Lamentations is a set of poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem (587 BC). It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. The "man" may be the prophet, or a voice representing the whole people. He speaks honestly from his pain, and the chapter then moves toward hope (3:21-23).

You can tell God sincerely how you feel when you suffer, without pretending to be strong. The Bible allows lament, and from that place of honesty hope in God's faithfulness can also grow.
exp.2:3:
It says that God made the speaker's body wear away: his flesh and his skin grew old and weak, and his bones were broken or crushed. It is strong language for a pain felt deep within the body.

The one speaking in the book is a poet who mourns for Jerusalem after its destruction. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so clearly. In this chapter he speaks as a wounded man who feels the hand of God heavy upon him, and his complaint also represents the suffering of the whole people.

For today: when pain drains you inside and out, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly how you feel, as this writer does. Later in this same chapter, the prayer moves toward hope.
exp.2:4:
He built a barrier against me, as one who builds a wall or fence around someone. He surrounded me with bitterness and sorrow. He also surrounded me with hardship, meaning weariness, grief, and suffering.

The one speaking is a poet who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the pain of his people. Tradition usually attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. In this chapter, the man describes his anguish as if God himself had turned against him. It is the language of sincere pain, not a complete explanation of who God is.

For today: when you feel that life is closing in on you with bitterness and exhaustion, you do not have to hide it. The Bible allows you to weep honestly before God. Tell him frankly what you feel; this same chapter, further on, reminds us that his mercies do not come to an end.
exp.2:5:
In this verse, the speaker, who is lamenting his suffering, says that God has made him live in darkness, like those who have been dead for ages. The darkness stands for suffering, sadness, and a lack of hope. The picture is of someone forgotten, shut away, and without light.

The book of Lamentations is a collection of poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text itself does not name him. Here a man brought low speaks, and he feels that God himself has struck him. He expresses his pain with raw honesty, as he feels it, rather than offering a complete explanation of God.

If you feel you are in darkness today, you can tell God honestly what you feel. The Bible allows prayer that includes complaint. And this poem does not end here: later in the same chapter, hope in God's mercy appears.
exp.2:7:
What it says: The speaker feels that God does not hear him. Although he cried out for help and raised his voice, he feels that God has shut out his prayer, as if unwilling to pay attention. Two of the source's quoted phrases and the note about an old spelling are not part of this verse, so they are left out here.

Context: Lamentations is a book of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. In this chapter, the speaker describes his pain with harsh images: darkness, chains, and blocked paths. He expresses how he feels, not necessarily the whole truth about God. Later in the same chapter, hope returns (3:21-26).

For today: If at some point you feel that God is keeping silent, do not hide your pain. You can tell him honestly, as this writer does. Praying without pretending is also faith. Keep crying out, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.2:8:
He has blocked the path of the one speaking with walls of cut and shaped stone, that is, large, firm stones that cannot be moved. He has also twisted his paths: he made them confusing and full of turns, so that he could not move forward with clarity.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He speaks in the midst of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. He feels enclosed, with no way out and no answer from God. It is language of complaint and suffering, expressed with strong images. Later in this same chapter, the tone shifts toward hope in God's mercy.

If today you feel that everything is closed off and you cannot see a way out, you can tell God so honestly, as this text does. Praying in pain is not a lack of faith. And keep reading: hope comes afterward.
exp.2:9:
In the grief of the one speaking, God seems to him like a bear lying in wait, ready to attack, or like a lion hidden in dark places.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. He speaks honestly from his suffering and feels that God is against him. This is his perception in the middle of pain, and the book later returns to hope in the faithfulness of God (3:21-26).

For today: when you feel that God is far away or is hard on you, you do not have to pretend. You can tell him honestly what you feel, as this writer does, and keep seeking him, trusting that his mercy does not run out.
exp.2:11:
He has drawn his bow, meaning he has readied it to shoot, and he has set me up as the target that the arrow is aimed at. The image is harsh: the writer feels that God has made him the mark of his attack.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. In this passage he speaks of his pain in very strong language, the way he feels it. Later in the same chapter, hope returns as he remembers the mercy of God.

Today, if you are going through suffering that makes you feel abandoned, you can tell God honestly what you feel, hiding nothing. The Bible allows sincere lament, and sometimes hope comes after we pour out our hearts in prayer.
exp.2:12:
God, like an archer, took the arrows he kept in his quiver (the case where arrows are carried) and drove them deep into the body of the one speaking. The arrows stand for pain, and the "kidneys" stand for the innermost part of a person: their feelings and their inner self.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Many believe it is Jeremiah, though the book does not say so openly. In this chapter he expresses his grief with very strong images, feeling that God himself has struck him. It is the honest language of someone who is suffering, not a complete explanation of who God is; later in the same chapter, hope in his mercy appears.

Today, if you are hurt, you can speak to God with complete honesty, without pretending. He hears the lament, and an honest prayer can be the way toward hope.
exp.2:14:
He says that God filled him with bitter things until he was satisfied. The words for being filled and made drunk in the verse refer to being filled completely and being made to drink until dizzy. Wormwood is a plant with a very bitter taste, a symbol of suffering and deep sorrow. It is an image of pain that leaves no room for anything else.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem and expresses his pain in the first person, perhaps as the voice of the whole people. He attributes his suffering to the hand of God, and speaks with raw honesty, without softening what he feels.

For today: you do not have to pretend that everything is fine before God. You can tell him sincerely how much something hurts you. Lamentations shows that honest complaint is also prayer, and later in this same chapter, hope returns.
exp.2:15:
It says that God, seen by the one who suffers as the one who strikes him, made him eat bread with bits of gravel, and his teeth were broken. The word "gravel" in the verse refers to small stones or coarse grit. He also covered him with ashes, a sign of mourning, sorrow, and humiliation.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah. He weeps over the fall of Jerusalem and over his own pain. He speaks in very strong language, as he feels it in the middle of his suffering. But the book does not end here: shortly afterward it remembers that God's mercies do not come to an end.

For today: when pain leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. Tell God honestly what you feel, as this passage does. And do not stop at the verse of discouragement; keep reading until you come to where hope returns.
exp.2:17:
It says that the one speaking feels he has no strength and no hope left. The phrase "my strength has perished" means that his spirit and his endurance are finished. And "my hope from the Lord" means that he no longer expects anything good to come from God. It is a very honest confession of complete discouragement.

The speaker is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the text does not say so clearly. He speaks after the destruction of Jerusalem and expresses his pain with harsh images: broken teeth, ashes, a lack of peace. Here we see him at his lowest point. But verse 21 later changes the tone: "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope."

For today: if you are exhausted and feel that hope has gone out, you can tell God exactly what you feel, as this author does. Praying honestly is not a lack of faith. And remember that pain does not always have the last word.
exp.2:21:
It says that we remain alive and have not been destroyed completely, thanks to God's mercy. The word for "consumed" in the verse means finished off or wholly destroyed. The word for "fail" means that something runs out or comes to an end. In other words, God's compassionate love never runs out.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so explicitly. He is grieving the destruction of Jerusalem. In the midst of deep pain, he chooses to remember who God is, and from that he draws hope. That is why, just before this, he says he will bring this to his heart so that he may wait.

For today: in difficult days, pause and remember how God has sustained you until now. Write down one or two times when his help came, and give him thanks. That strengthens hope for tomorrow.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that the author declares to himself that God is his "portion," that is, his inheritance, his share, the most valuable thing he has. For this reason he decides to wait on Him. The word that the verse renders as "Lord" is the name of God, and the word for waiting means to trust with patience. "Soul" here speaks of his whole being, of his inner self.

The speaker is a poet who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so explicitly. In the midst of his grief, he remembers the mercy of God and encourages himself not to lose hope. The word "portion" recalls that the Levites received no land, because God himself was their portion.

When everything seems lost, you can tell your soul that God is still enough. Today, instead of worrying, take a moment to thank Him for who He is and decide to wait on Him with calm.
exp.2:25:
It is good to wait quietly and patiently for God's salvation. "Salvation" here does not refer to bodily health, but to the rescue or deliverance that comes from the Lord. Waiting in this way means not complaining or giving up in despair, but waiting with patience and trust.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, in the midst of very great grief. Yet at this point he remembers that God is his portion and that He is good to those who seek Him. His hope comes from trusting the character of God, not from things looking better.

For today: when you are in a trial and see no way out, before reacting with anger or anxiety, pause for a few minutes in silence and pray. Remember that God is good, and trust that He is working even while you wait.
exp.2:26:
It is good for a person to learn to carry the yoke from a young age. The "yoke" was the wooden piece placed on animals for work; here it represents the burden, the discipline, or the suffering.

Lamentations reflects the grief over the destruction of Jerusalem (587 B.C.). Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not state this clearly. The speaker here, in the midst of his anguish, remembers that God is good and faithful. Many understand the yoke as the trials God allows; others, as discipline in general. The verses that follow speak of waiting in silence and with humility.

For today: do not flee from every difficulty, and do not grow bitter because of it. The trials of youth, such as effort, patience, and obedience, can form a steady character and a faith that trusts in God. When something weighs on you, pray and wait on Him.
exp.2:29:
The person who suffers, he says, will offer his cheek to the one who strikes him, and will be full of disgrace. That is, he will endure many insults and humiliations without answering with revenge.

Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Here a man speaks who has suffered greatly (tradition links him to Jeremiah, though the book does not give his name). He accepts the punishment in silence and humility, waiting on God. The verses that follow explain why: the Lord does not reject forever, and his compassion is great.

For today: when you are offended or treated unjustly, try not to respond with anger right away. Keep silent, pray, and trust that God is compassionate and can sustain you. This does not mean accepting abuse, but waiting on God without returning evil for evil.
exp.2:34:
He says that God sees and does not overlook it when someone takes away from a person their right, that is, what is justly due to them. Turning aside a man's right means bending justice. Before the face of the Most High means that this happens in plain view of God, who is the supreme God. The verse is part of a list of injustices that the Lord does not approve.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, a poet who mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. In the middle of his grief, he remembers that God governs and that he is not indifferent to abuse, unjust imprisonment, or twisted justice. There are different ways of understanding the passage, but the comfort is that God is watching.

For today: if you have been treated unjustly, or if you have power over others, remember that God sees. Bring your pain to him in prayer, and deal justly with those who depend on you.
exp.2:38:
This verse asks a question worth pondering: why should a person complain while still alive, when they are suffering the consequences of their own sin? The word for complaining here means to grumble with resentment, and the question points us toward a life that still has breath and, with it, a chance to respond.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not name him. Here the author acknowledges that God is sovereign and that the judgment was no accident. So instead of blaming God, he calls the people to examine themselves and return to Him.

For today: when difficulty comes, before you complain, pause and pray honestly. Ask God whether there is something you need to correct. Even in pain, the life you have is an opportunity to return to Him and receive His mercy.
exp.2:47:
He says the writer weeps without stopping, as though his eyes were rivers of water. The reason is the destruction of the daughter of his people, that is, the ruin and grief of his nation. "Daughter of my people" is a poetic way of speaking about the nation, with tenderness. The destruction here means ruin or a deep wound.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem, which was destroyed by the Babylonians. Its enemies mocked, and the people suffered. The verses that follow show that he waits until God looks down and sees from heaven.

Today we can weep with those who suffer, without offering hasty advice. And when the pain is great, we can bring those tears to God, trusting that He sees.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the gold, which was very valuable and bright, lost its shine and changed its appearance. The stones of the sanctuary, that is, of the temple, lie scattered at the corners and crossings of every street. What was beautiful and sacred has been destroyed and abandoned.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem, which was destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BC. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this explicitly. The speaker weeps over the ruin of the city. The gold may represent the temple or the people themselves, and the following verses speak of the sons of Zion, once treasured like gold.

For today: God invites us to be honest about our pain. If something you valued has collapsed, you can weep before Him without pretending. The Bible makes room for that lament.
exp.3:4:
They that ate the finest foods are now left destitute and ruined in the streets. Those who were raised in clothing dyed scarlet, a very costly red dye used by the wealthy, now cling to dunghills, that is, to heaps of refuse, searching for anything to survive.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He mourns for Jerusalem after the siege and the fall of the city to Babylon, around 586 B.C. The hunger was so terrible that not even the rich were spared. The book presents this as a consequence of the people's sin.

Today, this verse reminds us that wealth and comfort are not a secure foundation. We can be thankful for what we have, live it with humility, and share it with those in need, without waiting for hard times to arrive.
exp.3:13:
They wandered aimlessly through the streets, like blind people who stumble along. They were stained with blood, so filthy that no one wanted to touch their clothes. The phrase about stumbling means they staggered and wavered, and the word for stained means they were marked and made impure.

The one speaking is the poet of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. He blames above all the religious leaders, who were meant to guide the people but tolerated injustice and violence. The blood speaks of moral guilt, and the blindness speaks of having lost the guidance of God.

For today: those who lead others, in the church, in the family, or at work, carry a great responsibility. Let us ask God for integrity, and let us not forget to pray for our leaders. If we have failed, let us seek his forgiveness and his light.
exp.3:18:
It says that the enemies of Jerusalem were swifter than the eagles. They pursued them over the mountains and laid traps for them in the wilderness. Ambushes are surprise attacks launched from a hiding place. The point is that there was nowhere to run and no safe place.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. The people had hoped for help from allies who could not save them, and not even the king managed to escape.

When everything seems lost, it is wise not to place our hope in human resources that fail. We can be honest with God about our pain, as this book is, and seek in Him a refuge that does not disappoint us.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that the king of Judah, who was like the breath of life for the people, was captured by their enemies. The breath of our nostrils is the king, chosen by God. The people believed that under his protection they would live safely, even among the nations. The pits were hunting traps, and he was caught means that he was trapped.

The one speaking is the people of Jerusalem, mourning the fall of the city before Babylon in 586 BC. Many understand that it refers to King Zedekiah, who was captured after fleeing. His fall left the people without human hope. The book shows grief, but it also recognizes that God was at work in the judgment.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in leaders, institutions, or people, however good they may be. All of them can fail. We can thank them and pray for them, but our firmest trust must rest in God, who never falls.
exp.4:2:
They say the people feel like orphans, without a father to look after them, and that their mothers have become like widows, without a husband to protect them. It is a figure of speech: it describes helplessness, poverty, and lack of protection.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who cry out to God after the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile. They lost their lands and homes, and they live under foreign rule. Many believe that many men died in the war, which is why there are so many widows. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. It is a prayer of sincere pain.

For today: when you feel alone or without support, you can speak to God with complete honesty, as this people does. And if you know someone who is an orphan or a widow, reach out with concrete help: a visit, a meal, or a friendly hand.
exp.4:11:
This verse says the enemies hanged the princes, that is, the leaders of the people. This may mean they were hanged by their hands, or that they were executed by order of the invaders; scholars understand it in several ways. Also, they did not honour the elders: the phrase about not honouring the faces of the old men means that they gave them no honour at all.

Here the people of Judah speak in prayer. Lamentations 5 is a cry after the fall of Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so. The people describe their humiliation: hunger, violence and the loss of their leaders, and they bring it before God.

For today: when the pain is so great that there are no words, we can speak to God with complete sincerity. And we should honour and care for the elderly, for God values them.
exp.4:12:
They were forced to grind grain, a heavy task usually done by slaves or women, and the boys were made to carry wood until they collapsed from exhaustion.

The speaker is the people of Judah, praying after the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Lamentations is a song of grief. Here they describe how the defeat destroyed the honor and strength of a whole generation, including the young men. Scholars often attribute the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: God does not ignore those who carry unjust burdens. We can help someone who is worn out, especially the young, and bring our weariness to God with sincerity.
exp.4:13:
It says that the elders no longer sit at the city gate, and that the young men have stopped singing. The word "young men" here refers to the men who are young. In that time, the gate was the place where the elders gathered to give counsel, settle disputes, and look after the life of the people.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after it was destroyed by the Babylonians. Without its leaders and its joy, the city fell into silence. The people acknowledge that they suffer because of their sin (v. 16).

For today: when sadness silences the music of your life, do not keep it quiet. Bring it before God with sincerity, as this book does. And value the elders who give counsel and the young people who bring joy.
exp.4:14:
What it says: The people confess that there is no longer any joy in their hearts. That festive dance has turned into mourning, that is, into sorrow and grief over a great loss.

Context: Lamentations is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem, probably after the Babylonian invasion. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. Here the suffering community speaks: the young men labor as slaves, the elders no longer gather at the city gate, and the music has stopped. The verses that follow acknowledge that sin played a part in this tragedy.

For today: When pain comes, there is no need to pretend to be joyful. You can bring your sadness to God with honesty, as this people does. Lamenting before Him is a form of faith, because it trusts that God listens and can restore.
exp.4:15:
The crown, which was a sign of honor, dignity and blessing, has fallen from the head of the people. That is why they weep: their cry of pain is the heart of the verse. They also admit their guilt, saying that they have sinned. The young men are the youths, and the circle was the ring of people who danced and celebrated.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the fall of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. Here the people speak, looking at the ruins, the sadness, and the silence where there used to be festivity. They do not blame only others; they admit their sin.

For today: when something collapses in your life, ask God to show you honestly what part of it you need to acknowledge. This is not meant to drown you in guilt, but to bring you back to Him, who forgives and restores.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that Mount Zion is "desolate," that is, destroyed and abandoned. That is why foxes roam there freely, as in a place with no people. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood.

The people of Judah speak in Lamentations, a book of mourning that is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. It was written after Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon, in 586 BC. The people acknowledge their sin and weep. The foxes show that the holy place was left empty and in ruins. Then, in the next verse, the prayer turns again toward God, who reigns forever.

For today: when you see ruins in your life, do not hide them. Bring them honestly before God, and remember that his throne does not fall, even when everything else does.
exp.1:21:
He says that God summoned terrors from every side, as people are summoned to an appointed feast. On the day of the LORD's anger, no one escaped or survived. The children the speaker cared for and raised, the enemy destroyed. The verse of the verse's wording, which uses "those I nurtured and reared," also applies here: the children were the ones the speaker had nurtured, and the enemy destroyed them completely.

The poet speaking in Lamentations is traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. He mourns Jerusalem, destroyed by Babylon in 586 B.C. He understands it as God's judgment for the people's sin, and so he uses the image of a feast: God himself summoned the disaster. It is a lament full of pain, not a cold explanation.

For today: when the pain is very great, you can bring it to God honestly, without pretending. He allows his people to speak to him with tears, and he also hears the cry of the one who suffers.
exp.2:30:
It says that the Lord will not reject or abandon his people forever. "Cast off" means to reject or push something aside, and "forever" indicates that this rejection will not be final. The pain may be real, but it has a limit.

The one speaking in Lamentations is a poet mourning the destruction of Jerusalem, probably at the time of the Babylonian conquest. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the book does not state this explicitly. In chapter 3, in the midst of his anguish, the author remembers who God is and holds on to hope. The verses that follow explain that, although God brings affliction, he also shows compassion.

Today, when you go through a painful season, do not interpret it as the end of your story with God. Tell him honestly what you feel, and remember his past mercies. His silence or his discipline are not eternal abandonment.
exp.2:53:
It says that the speaker felt covered by a flood, with the water going over his head, and thought it was the end.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. In this chapter he speaks as a man who suffers, pursued by enemies without cause, trapped like a bird and shut up in a prison. Some read it as his personal pain and others as the voice of the people of Jerusalem after its fall. Both readings are possible.

For today: when you feel that everything is overwhelming you, you can tell God honestly what you feel, even "I thought I was going to die." This man said it and then prayed. God does not turn away from one who cries out from the depths.
exp.0:8:
Her uncleanness stains her skirts, like a mark that cannot be washed out. The text says she did not think about where all this would lead, that is, her final outcome or her future. Because of that, her fall is shocking, and there is no one to comfort her. At the end, someone cries out to God: "Look, O LORD, on my affliction," because the enemy has triumphed.

This is the book of Lamentations, a song of grief after the destruction of Jerusalem. The poet speaks first, describing the city as a humbled woman, and in this part the city itself prays. The text links her fall with her sin, though not every detail of that time is told here.

For today: let us not ignore the consequences of our decisions, but let us also not stop praying. When you are wounded, even by your own mistakes, you can say honestly to God: "Look, O LORD, on my affliction."
exp.4:8:
This verse says that the people had to risk their lives just to get food. "We get our bread" means that they went out to search for or gather food. "The sword in the wilderness" is a poetic way of speaking of the sword: the dangers from outside, such as armed gangs or thieves. Some think it may also refer to the heat and threat of the desert; the text allows both ideas.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. The speaker is the people of Judah, who describe their suffering after the destruction. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. With sorrow, they acknowledge the consequences of sin and the loss of security under the rule of strangers.

For today: if you know someone who works in fear or needs to support their family, do not walk past. Pray for that person and help them in a concrete way, with food, work, or companionship.
exp.0:21:
The passage says that God should take notice of all the wickedness of the enemies and treat them as he has treated the one speaking, because of that person's rebellions. The words "Let all their wickedness come before You" mean "let it come before your presence." "Groans" are cries of deep sorrow. The one speaking confesses that his heart is sick with sadness.

Jerusalem speaks here, pictured as an afflicted woman, at the end of the first lament. The city was destroyed and its people carried into exile. She acknowledges that her own rebellion against God brought the punishment, but she also sees that her neighbors mocked her fall. For this reason she asks for justice. It is an honest cry, and scholars understand it as prayer, not as personal revenge.

Today we can bring our pain to God with complete sincerity, acknowledging our failures without hiding them, and leave justice in his hands instead of taking it ourselves.
exp.2:52:
This verse says that the speaker was dropped alive into a deep pit and that stones were thrown down on him. A pit like this is a place of darkness and danger, and being dropped into it suggests he was trapped with no clear way to climb out. The stones piled on him give the sense of being buried alive, with no way out.

Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. The speaker expresses his grief in a personal way, and it is not clear whether he refers to his own experience, to that of Jeremiah (whom tradition links to the book), or to that of the whole people. His enemies hunted him without cause, like someone hunting a bird. That is why the next verse speaks of waters covering him and of calling on God from the depths.

When you feel shut in and without a way out, do not keep your pain silent. Cry out to God with sincerity, as this man did, because He hears even from the darkest place.
exp.2:55:
Here the speaker remembers that God already heard him when he cried out from a very dark place. Now he asks God not to ignore his cry for relief. The phrase "do not ignore my cry" means do not look away from my pleading, do not pretend you have not heard me. The word "relief" points to the rest and freedom from distress that he longs for.

The speaker is the poet of Lamentations, who suffers in the midst of Jerusalem's ruin. He speaks in the first person, perhaps for himself or on behalf of his people; this is debated. His words come from an anguish so great that he feels drowned by waters and shut in a deep prison, yet he remembers that God has answered before.

For today: when you are overwhelmed, remember how God helped you before, and pray with that confidence. Ask Him for relief sincerely, without pretending to a strength you do not have.
exp.0:9:
The enemy has reached out to seize everything of value in Jerusalem. The city watched in grief as foreign nations entered the sanctuary, the temple, even though God had forbidden them to enter his assembly. The treasures described here are precious possessions, most likely those of the temple and the city.

The poet of Lamentations speaks, weeping for Jerusalem, and in other verses the city itself speaks. It is a song of mourning over the destruction of the city by Babylon in 586 B.C. The text says this happened because of the people's sin. Even so, the writer does not stay silent: he cries out to God and asks him to look upon their affliction.

For today: when you suffer because of your mistakes or because of things you have lost, do not hide from God. You can bring him your pain honestly, acknowledge what you did wrong, and ask him to look upon you with compassion.
exp.3:8:
It says that it was better to die in war, by the sword, than to die of hunger. Whoever dies by the sword is soon finished; whoever dies of hunger wastes away slowly, pierced with pain, because the fields no longer produced food. "Pierced with pain" describes that slow suffering, and "the fields lack produce" refers to the failed harvests that left people with nothing to eat.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. The verses before describe how hunger disfigured even the healthiest and most distinguished people. The poet sees this suffering as part of God's judgment on the people's sin.

For today: do not minimize the long, quiet suffering of others. There are slow pains, such as poverty or illness, that need our constant compassion. And you can bring your laments to God with sincerity, as this book does.
exp.2:18:
Here the speaker asks God to remember his suffering. "Affliction" means pain and hardship, and "wandering" points to the sense of being lost or driven away from home and peace. The "wormwood" is a very bitter plant, and "gall" is another bitter taste, used as an image of a life full of bitterness.

Lamentations is a book of mourning over the fall of Jerusalem. The speaker (tradition says it is Jeremiah, though the book does not state this) feels without peace, without strength, and almost without hope. But remembering his pain leads him, in the verses that follow, to remember the faithfulness of God and to decide to wait.

For today: you can be honest with God about your sadness, without disguising it. Tell Him in simple words what embitters you. Praying this way is not a lack of faith; often it is the first step toward waiting on Him again.
exp.2:43:
He says that God has wrapped himself in a cloud, like a thick curtain, so that no prayer can get through to him. The phrase "no prayer can pass through" is an image: the people feel that God has closed the way and is not listening to them.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations (tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so). He speaks on behalf of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. He acknowledges his rebellion, but he also expresses his pain and his sense of being abandoned. It is the honest complaint of someone who suffers the consequences of his sin.

There are times when God seems silent and prayer feels empty. This verse shows that we can express that feeling with sincerity. Even so, the book moves on and arrives at hope: "his mercies are new every morning" (3:23). Keep praying, even when you feel no answer.
exp.2:2:
He says that God keeps turning His hand against the one who is speaking, again and again, without stopping. The phrase "all day long" means that from morning to night this man feels the weight of God's hand. It is not a single blow, but a pain that seems to repeat itself without rest.

The one speaking is a man who suffers greatly, probably after the destruction of Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not give the name. Here the poet expresses his pain with honesty and feels that God himself is against him. This is his perception in the midst of pain; later in the chapter hope appears.

Today, if you are suffering, you can speak to God with sincerity, without pretending to be strong. Expressing your anguish in prayer is a way of continuing to trust in Him.
exp.4:19:
The verse says that the people ask God in pain: "Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?" The phrase "for so long" points to a very extended period. It is not that God really forgets, but that this is how his absence is felt.

Lamentations is a song of sorrow. The people of Judah speak after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, probably by the Babylonians. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. Just before this verse, the people remember that God reigns forever, and that is why they dare to ask and to plead for restoration.

For today: when you feel forgotten by God, do not keep your pain silent. You can honestly bring him your questions, while also remembering that he remains faithful. Sincere prayer, even with tears, is a form of trust.
exp.2:44:
This verse says that God made his people "scum and refuse" among the nations. "Scum" is what rises to the surface and is skimmed off and thrown away, like trash or waste. "Refuse" is what is rejected and discarded. "You have made us" means "you have made us into." It is a very harsh image: they feel despised by everyone.

The speaker of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly, mourns on behalf of the people after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon (587-586 B.C.). He interprets the suffering as the consequence of God's judgment, and he feels that his prayers do not reach God.

Today, when you feel despised or cast aside, you can bring your pain to God with complete honesty, without pretending. This book shows that lamenting is also a form of faith, since it keeps speaking with God.
exp.4:1:
Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, and our houses to foreigners. This verse says that the land and the homes God had given Israel as a family possession now belong to others. An inheritance is property that is passed down from one's parents, and strangers and foreigners are people from outside, who are not part of the nation.

The wording "has been turned over" in the verse is the way the loss is described, as something handed from one owner to another.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who pray to God after the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. The people suffer the loss of their land, their security and their dignity, and they ask God to remember and to look upon their shame.

For today: when you feel you have lost something important, such as a home, a job or stability, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God honestly, as this people does. Sincere prayer is the first step toward finding comfort and hope.
exp.1:6:
The Lord himself has rejected his altar and abandoned his sanctuary, the temple in Jerusalem. He allowed the enemy to take the walls of the palaces. "They have raised a shout" means that the enemies shouted inside the house of the Lord, just as the people once shouted with joy on the appointed feast days. What was once a sound of worship has become the shouting of an enemy's victory.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not name him. The poet understands the fall as the result of God's judgment for the people's sin, and for that reason he speaks of God as the one who has turned against the city.

For today: when worship becomes routine or merely for show, God is not satisfied with ceremonies alone. We can ask him for a sincere heart, and remember that, even in pain, the poet still addresses God.
exp.2:63:
The speaker asks God to pay his enemies back for the wrong they have done, giving them what they deserve for their actions. Here the phrase is rendered in plain modern terms as "you will pay them back what they deserve," and "the work of their hands" refers to what they have done.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He speaks in the middle of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. He feels persecuted, mocked all day long, turned into a song of ridicule. He did not take revenge himself; he brought his complaint to God and asked him for justice.

For today: when someone has hurt you, you can honestly tell God your pain and leave justice in his hands, instead of seeking revenge. Jesus also teaches us to pray for those who harm us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.2:50:
What the author saw with his own eyes brought him a very deep pain in his soul. The phrase "bring grief to my soul" means that what he witnessed filled him with sorrow and anguish. "The daughters of my city" refers to the women of Jerusalem, and some believe it also includes the other towns and villages of Judah. It was a pain caused by what they were suffering.

The poet of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, speaks here. Jerusalem had been destroyed, and the people suffered hunger, violence and captivity. He weeps without stopping and hopes that God will look down from heaven. Some think he speaks for himself and for the whole people.

For today: do not close your eyes to the pain of others. Let their suffering move you to pray, to stand with them and to help in whatever way you can. And as you weep, hand that sadness over to God, who does see and does have compassion.
exp.0:11:
It says that Jerusalem, speaking like a wounded person, calls out to everyone who passes by on the road. She asks them whether her suffering means nothing to them, and urges them to look closely: is there any pain like hers? She acknowledges that this pain comes from the LORD, who inflicted it on her on the day of his fierce anger. The sentence about "means nothing to them" is explained as "it matters to you" or "it touches your heart." The word for "fierce anger" refers to intense, burning wrath.

The speaker is Jerusalem, pictured as a woman. The book mourns the destruction of the city, probably by the Babylonians, in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so. The people have lost their wealth, have seen their temple invaded, and are going hungry. She understands that this is the consequence of her rebellion.

When you suffer, do not keep it in silence. Tell God your pain honestly, as this book does, and seek out people who will listen. And if you see someone suffering, do not walk past: stop and stand with them.
exp.2:16:
It says the suffering was so strong that the person felt peace had been taken far away from their life. "My soul has been deprived of peace" means they lost their calm and their quiet. "I have forgotten what prosperity is" means they no longer remembered what was good, and could not feel that anything good existed.

The one speaking in this chapter is a man describing his grief after the destruction of Jerusalem. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. He speaks of bitterness and ruin, and in the verses that follow he admits that he nearly lost hope in God. But then he recalls the faithfulness of the Lord (v. 21-23).

When pain makes us forget what is good, we are not alone, and we are not poor believers for feeling it. We can do as he did: tell God honestly how we feel, and then calmly remember some of his past kindnesses, even if it is just one.
exp.2:28:
He bends low to the ground, with his face buried in the dust, as a sign of humility and surrender. He does this because he is not sure how everything will turn out, yet he still waits on God, perhaps there is still hope.

Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. Tradition ascribes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this directly. In chapter 3, the speaker moves from pain to trust that the Lord does not abandon forever. This verse describes an attitude of humility in the midst of suffering, not a call to give in to evil.

When you go through a trial you do not understand, you can come to God with humility and honesty, without pretending to be strong. Tell Him your pain, rest in Him, and keep hope alive, even when you cannot yet see the end.
exp.2:32:
It says that God does not take pleasure in causing people to suffer. Here "afflict" means causing pain, and "grieve" means causing deep anguish. The verse says God does not do this willingly or gladly. God may allow pain, but he does not delight in it.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem, but in the midst of his pain he remembers that God is faithful and compassionate. This verse explains the one before it: if God corrects, he also shows mercy. The verses that follow speak of injustices that the Lord sees.

If you are going through a trial today, do not think that God rejoices in your suffering. You can pray honestly, tell him about your distress, and trust that his compassion remains with you, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.3:17:
They stalked our every step, so that we could not walk in our streets. The enemies watched the people of Jerusalem like hunters following their prey, and the residents could no longer move about their own city in safety. "They stalked our every step" means that they spied on them and lay in wait for them. "Our end drew near" speaks of the end of the city, and "our time ran out" means that their time had come to an end.

The poet of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, mourns with his people the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The verses nearby mention a hope placed in allies who could not save them, and the text sees this as a consequence of the people's sin.

For today: when everything falls apart, it is wise to stop trusting human supports that fail. We can be honest with God in our pain, as this poet is, and place our hope in Him again.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that Jerusalem, called "Daughter of Zion", has lost all her splendor. "Splendor" refers to her glory, her peace and her dignity. Her leaders, that is, her rulers, have become like deer that find no pasture. They lack the strength to flee, and so they fall before the one who hunts them, that is, before the enemy who pursues them.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book itself does not give his name. Here the poet speaks, mourning the ruined city. The text explains this ruin as the consequence of the people's rebellions against God, but it does so with deep sorrow, not with coldness.

For today: when life falls apart, we can bring our pain to God with honesty. Acknowledging our mistakes and grieving without pretending to be strong is a step toward hope.
exp.2:1:
It says that God drove him away and made him walk in darkness instead of light. The phrase "made me walk" describes a path through pain, confusion, and having no sense of direction. The "darkness" stands for that same suffering.

The one speaking is a man who suffers greatly, and so he says: "I am the one who has seen affliction." The book of Lamentations mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not name him. Some think this "man" represents the whole people. He feels that God's punishment weighs on him, and he speaks with sincerity and pain.

For today: when you pass through a dark season, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can tell God honestly what you feel. This chapter does not end in darkness; later it speaks of the faithfulness of God (3:22-23).
exp.4:6:
Our ancestors sinned and are gone, and now we are the ones who bear the consequences of what they did. The phrase "are no more" in the verse means "they are gone," and the verse's words "but we bear their punishment" mean that the people carry the weight of that suffering.

The speakers are the people of Judah in Lamentations 5, a communal prayer after the fall of Jerusalem. They are humbled, poor, and ruled by others. They feel the pain of inheriting the results of earlier wrongs. Some scholars note that other biblical texts show each generation was also responsible for its own sin (Ezekiel 18). Here the people simply voice their complaint and their sorrow.

For today: we can be honest with God about the wounds we inherit, such as broken families or bad habits. We can also ask him to break that cycle in us, and begin, with his help, to choose a different path for those who come after us.
exp.2:56:
This verse says that on the same day the author called upon God, God drew near to him and answered, "Do not be afraid." The phrase "You drew near," in the verse you read, makes this plain, so no note about older forms of words is needed here. "When I called on You" means "when I called out" or "when I asked for help." God did not stay far away; he made himself present and gave calm.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. In this passage he speaks from a deep pit, which can be understood either as a real prison or as an image of extreme distress. He remembers that God had already heard him before, and so he dares to keep crying out.

For today: when you feel fear, speak with God honestly, even with only a few words. Then remember other times when he sustained you, and let his "Do not be afraid" calm your heart.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that the people feel God has rejected them completely and remains angry with them beyond measure. The phrase "utterly rejected us" means "you have cast us far away without wanting to know anything about us." The word "angry" describes God's strong displeasure. Some read the verse as a question or a doubt: "Have you rejected us completely?" The original language allows more than one reading.

The people speaking are the people of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem, probably in exile or among the ruins. Lamentations ends with a painful prayer. Just before it they ask: "Turn us back to you, O LORD, and we shall be turned." They acknowledge that they are suffering, but they do not stop crying out to God. The book does not end with a clear answer, but with an open plea.

When you feel far from God or hurt, do not keep silent. You can tell him honestly what you feel, even your doubts, and ask him to draw you close to himself. Honest prayer is also faith.
exp.3:5:
It says that the punishment of Jerusalem, called "the daughter of my people," was greater than that of Sodom. Sodom was overthrown in an instant, and no hand was turned to help her. Jerusalem, by contrast, endured a long and painful punishment. "Overthrown" means that she was destroyed.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, though the book does not say so, speaks here. He mourns for Jerusalem after she was besieged and destroyed by Babylon. The verses around it describe the terrible hunger: children without bread and the wealthy reduced to misery. The poet recognizes that this suffering is tied to the sin of the people.

For today: we can learn to see the consequences of sin with humility, without excuses. If there is something God points out to you, do not wait for the pain to grow; return to Him soon, for his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.3:11:
No one in the world, neither the kings nor ordinary people, thought that an enemy could ever get through the gates of Jerusalem. The city seemed safe. The verse uses two words for the attacker, enemy and foe, which together stress that the threat was real and that people were sure it could never happen. The phrase "any people of the world" refers to all the nations that were known at the time.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations. A tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The verses that follow explain that it happened because of the sins of the people's leaders, which made the surprise even more painful.

For today: let us not trust that something is secure just because it has always been that way. Our true security lies in living with humility and faithfulness before God, and in listening to his correction in time.
exp.0:2:
Judah has gone into exile under suffering and harsh slavery. She lives among the nations but finds no place to rest. All her pursuers have caught up with her in the middle of her distress, leaving her no way out.

Here the author of Lamentations speaks. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. The verses that follow explain that God allowed this affliction because of the people's many rebellions.

For today: when you go through times of anguish, do not face them in silence or alone. This book shows us that one can grieve honestly before God. Tell him your pain, acknowledge whatever you need to correct, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.0:4:
Her foes now rule over her, and her enemies live at ease while she suffers. "Her foes have become her masters" means they are now in charge and hold power over her. "Enemies" are the ones who hated her. "At ease" means they have been living comfortably. The text states that the LORD brought her grief because of her many "transgressions," that is, because she went against Him. Even her children were taken away as captives before the enemy.

The book is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem, probably before Babylon in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so clearly. Here a poet mourns for the city and acknowledges that the punishment came because of the sin of the people.

For today: when you face painful consequences of your own mistakes, do not harden yourself or blame others. Be honest with God, acknowledge your fault, and trust that He can restore you.
exp.3:20:
It says that Edom, which rejoiced to see Jerusalem fall, will not escape. "Daughter of Edom" refers to the people of Edom, a neighbor of Judah. "Uz" was a region linked to Edom, though its exact location is debated. The "cup" represents God's judgment, and "you will get drunk" means that Edom will receive it until it staggers. "Expose yourself" shows a shameful fall. The tone is ironic: "rejoice" is almost mocking.

The poet of Lamentations speaks on behalf of a people wounded by the fall of Jerusalem (around 586 B.C.). Tradition usually attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so. Edom had celebrated Judah's misfortune. The following verse promises that Zion's punishment will end and that Edom will answer for its sins.

Today: do not rejoice when someone falls, even if they have hurt you. Place your pain and your desire for justice in God's hands, and ask him for a compassionate heart.
exp.2:27:
This verse says that the person who suffers will sit alone and be quiet, because the LORD has laid this burden on him, a heavy weight. The phrase "sit alone in silence" describes withdrawing from others and holding one's tongue, and the phrase "the LORD has laid it upon him" means that the suffering has been placed on his shoulders.

The one speaking in this chapter is a man who suffers deeply after the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this directly. He describes his pain, but in the midst of it he remembers that God is faithful and that it is worth waiting on Him with humility.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not rush to complain to everyone. Find a quiet moment alone, still your anxiety, and pray calmly, waiting on God. Silence is not giving up, but trusting that He is at work even when we cannot see it.
exp.2:33:
This verse speaks of crushing underfoot all the prisoners of the land. "Crushing" means grinding down or trampling with cruelty, and "prisoners" are those who are held captive, often without any way to defend themselves. Together with the verses that follow, it forms a list of injustices that the Lord sees and does not approve.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. In the middle of his grief over the fall of Jerusalem, he recalls that God does not take pleasure in afflicting. Many understand the passage to affirm that God does not agree with oppression; others read it as rhetorical questions. Both readings agree on the essentials.

Today we can remember that God takes notice of those who suffer injustice. This invites us not to be indifferent: to pray for prisoners and the oppressed, and to treat with justice and compassion those who depend on our decisions.
exp.3:9:
The hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children, and those children became their food when Jerusalem was destroyed. This verse describes women once known for their tenderness and mercy who, in the horror of the famine, boiled and ate their own sons and daughters. The phrase "the daughter of my people" refers to Jerusalem and its people.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally linked to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the terrible famine during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The text shows the horror of God's judgment on the people's persistent sin, something already warned about in Deuteronomy 28:53.

For today: extreme pain can distort even what is most sacred. That is why we should help those who suffer hunger or crisis, and not ignore the sin that destroys what we love. Come to God with honesty, for He hears even the darkest lament.
exp.2:59:
It says that God has seen everything the enemies have done to harm. "Malice" here means the desire to pay back evil, the bitterness with which they attack. "Plots" are the schemes and hidden intentions. The speaker says to God: "You have seen all their malice, all their plots against me."

The speaker in Lamentations is a poet who suffers greatly after the destruction of Jerusalem. He is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so openly. In this chapter, he remembers how God rescued him and asks him to keep defending his cause against those who hate and persecute him without reason.

When someone treats you unjustly or speaks badly of you, you do not have to take revenge or prove your innocence at all costs. You can bring that pain to God in prayer, with honesty, and trust that he sees everything, even what no one else knows, and that he is a just judge.
exp.3:6:
This verse describes the dignitaries of Jerusalem as people who were brighter than snow and whiter than milk, with a healthy ruddy look that was more striking than rubies, and an appearance like sapphires. Here "dignitaries" probably refers to people who were set apart or honored, though some think it speaks of princes or nobles. The phrase "their bodies" refers to their physical form and bearing, meaning their appearance and figure.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem and recalls how the best of the people once were, to show the contrast with the hunger and ruin that came afterward, as the following verses say.

For today: health, reputation, or position can change suddenly. Let us not place our security in what can be lost, but in God, who remains faithful even in times of sorrow.
exp.2:64:
This verse says that the author asks God to place a veil of anguish over his enemies' hearts, and to let God's curse fall on them. The phrase "a veil of anguish over their hearts" can be understood as a covering of pain, hardness, or blindness that keeps the heart from seeing clearly. The Hebrew here is difficult, so the meaning is read in several ways.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He is suffering mockery and persecution, and "their song" refers to the theme of their mockery. After the fall of Jerusalem, he cries out to God to do justice and not to take vengeance himself.

For today: when you are wounded unjustly, you can bring your pain and your anger honestly to God, leaving justice in his hands. Jesus, moreover, teaches us to pray for those who harm us.
exp.4:18:
It says that, although everything around them has fallen, God does not change. "You reign forever" means that He is still the same and never ceases to rule. "Your throne" speaks of His authority as King, and "endures from generation to generation" means that His reign lasts through all ages, without interruption.

The people of Judah speak in a lament after the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple, probably at the hands of the Babylonians. They see Mount Zion in ruins, with foxes walking among the rubble. They are sad and confused. Yet, in the midst of their pain, they look to God and cling to the fact that He still reigns. For that reason, they soon ask Him to restore them.

For today: when you lose something important or feel without direction, you do not have to pretend that you are fine. You can tell God your pain honestly, while remembering that He is still on His throne. That truth does not take away the sadness, but it does give you a firm place to lean.
exp.2:57:
He says God stepped in like a lawyer for the one who suffers. Where the verse says "You defend my cause," it means you argued his case and stood up for him. "My cause" means my case, my deepest need. "You redeem my life" means you rescued my life from death or danger, like someone who pays to set another person free.

The author of Lamentations speaks here, perhaps Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. After the fall of Jerusalem, he speaks of his grief and of his enemies. Here he looks back and remembers that God heard him when he cried out and said to him, "Fear not." That memory gives him encouragement to keep asking for help.

When you are distressed, remember the times God has sustained you. That memory can give you courage to pray again and to trust that He defends your cause.
exp.3:15:
It says that the presence of the LORD has scattered the people of Jerusalem and that he no longer regards them with favor. The people gave no honor to the priests, and the elders found no favor among them. The phrase about scattering means that they were driven apart and sent away from their homeland. The phrase about honor means that the priests and elders were treated without respect or kindness.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 BC. The verses before this one describe the guilt of leaders, priests, and prophets. Some understand the lack of honor to refer to the enemies, and others to the inhabitants of Jerusalem themselves. The text allows both readings.

Today it reminds us that God cares how we treat others, especially those who are older and those who serve. Today you can honor an elder with a visit, a phone call, or your time.
exp.1:7:
It says that God himself decided to tear down the walls of Jerusalem, called "the Daughter of Zion." The phrase "He stretched out a measuring line" pictures a builder with a cord, but here it describes tearing down with precision. The outer wall in front of the main wall is the low barrier before the principal wall. Both walls mourn and waste away together, as if the city itself were weeping.

Lamentations is a funeral song for the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. The poet sees the destruction as the result of God's judgment on the people's persistent sin, and he expresses it with pain, not with coldness.

For today: when we go through losses, we can bring our pain to God honestly, without pretending. Lamenting is also a form of faith, because we keep speaking with Him, and the book later speaks of His mercy that is renewed every morning.
exp.2:13:
The verse says that the speaker has become a laughingstock to all his people. They mock him in song all day long. The word "laughingstock" means someone who is ridiculed or scorned. He has become the subject of their mocking songs, the theme of their jeering chants, and this goes on every day without rest.

The speaker in Lamentations is a poet who suffers while Jerusalem lies in ruins, probably after the Babylonian invasion. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. In this passage, he feels that God himself has wounded him, like an archer aiming an arrow. To that pain is added the shame before his own people.
