For today: if you are in pain and the mockery of others weighs on you, you can be honest with God, as this poet is. The Bible allows us to weep and complain in prayer. And later in this same chapter, hope returns as he remembers the faithfulness of God.
exp.0:6:
In the days of her affliction and wandering, Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old. When her people fell into enemy hands, she received no help, and her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall. Her "treasures" are her blessings and the precious things she once had. To "laugh at" someone is to mock them with scorn. The mockery was directed at her downfall, the collapse of the city and its people.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem, most likely in 586 B.C. at the hands of Babylon. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text itself does not state this clearly. Here the city is pictured as a wandering, abandoned woman who, in her loneliness, remembers what she has lost and acknowledges that her rebellions had consequences.

For today: When we go through difficult times, we can pause honestly, acknowledge our mistakes without sinking into guilt, and turn to God, who hears those who cry out to Him.
exp.3:2:
This verse compares the animals with the mothers of Jerusalem. Even the jackals offer their breasts and nurse their young. But the women of the city, because of extreme hunger, could not do this and seemed cruel, like the ostrich in the wilderness, which was said to neglect its young. The word for the mother's breast in the verse is "breast," and the little ones are the babies.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, though the book does not say so. He mourns for Jerusalem after it was destroyed by Babylon. The hunger of the siege was so terrible that families were torn apart. He does not accuse harshly but expresses grief.

For today: when you see extreme suffering, do not judge it coldly. Pray, help with what you can, and trust that God sees the pain of the smallest.
exp.1:2:
In his fierce anger, God has cut off every horn of Israel. The horn was a symbol of strength, like that of a bull. The verse also says that God has withdrawn his right hand, that is, his hand of protection, as the enemy approached. His anger has burned in Jacob, that is, among the people, like a flaming fire that consumes everything around it.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, speaks here. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem before Babylon, in the year 586 BC. He understands this ruin as the consequence of God's judgment for the people's sin, and he describes it with grief.

Today we can learn to be honest with God in our pain, without hiding our tears. This book teaches us to lament before Him, and to keep seeking Him even when everything seems lost, trusting that his mercy does not run out (Lamentations 3:22-23).
exp.2:6:
It says that God, from the viewpoint of the one who suffers, has walled him in so that he cannot escape, and has weighed him down with chains. The image is of a prisoner who is hemmed in on every side and cannot find a way out. The chains are the heavy burden placed on him, the sense of being bound and held down.

The one speaking is a man who lives through the grief of the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition usually attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so clearly. Here he speaks in the language of complaint, like someone who feels God is against him. It is the feeling of the one who suffers, not a complete explanation of who God is. The same chapter later speaks of hope in the mercy of the Lord.

For today: if you feel trapped and without a way out, you can tell God honestly what you feel, even the rawest things. The Bible makes room for that honesty, and from there one can go on waiting on Him.
exp.0:7:
Jerusalem sinned greatly, and so she has become an object of scorn. The people who once respected her now look down on her, because they have seen her nakedness, meaning her shame and public humiliation. She groans in pain and turns away.

The book mourns the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text does not state this clearly. Here the poet speaks, describing the city as a wounded woman and acknowledging that her suffering is tied to her sin and rebellion.

For today: when we fail, it is not good to hide our shame or blame others. We can acknowledge the truth with humility and cry out to God, for the same book later reminds us that his mercies never end.
exp.2:49:
The speaker says he will keep weeping until the LORD looks down from heaven and sees. That is, his weeping will not stop until God notices his pain and acts. "Looks down and sees" expresses that God pays attention and intervenes, not merely that he observes.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, whom tradition identifies with Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. He weeps over the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. His tears do not stop because he finds no relief, and he waits for God to respond.

Today we can bring our pain to God honestly, without hiding it. Weeping before Him is not a lack of faith; it is waiting for Him to see us. You can pray sincerely and trust that He hears, even when the answer takes time.
exp.2:37:
It says that everything that happens is under the authority of God, the Most High. It asks whether both adversity and good do not come from his mouth. The word "adversity" here refers to hardships or misfortunes, not to moral wickedness. The verse before it asks who can say that something happened without the Lord permitting or commanding it.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. In the midst of the pain, he acknowledges that God governs even the suffering of the people. Then he invites us to examine our own lives and return to the LORD, without complaining against Him.

For today: when a difficulty comes, instead of complaining bitterly, stop and pray. Ask God to show you whether there is something to correct, and trust that He is still good and still hears you.
exp.3:3:
This verse describes the suffering of infants during the famine. The nursing baby's tongue clings to the roof of its mouth from thirst, because it no longer receives milk. Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any. The image of breaking bread into pieces and sharing it with each child shows what is missing here: there is no one to do it.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so explicitly. He mourns for Jerusalem after the siege and the fall of the city. He compares mothers to ostriches, which were described as careless with their young, to show that the hunger was so severe that normal care had broken down. The poet understands this suffering as a consequence of the people's sin.

Today we can think of the smallest and most vulnerable people around us. God grieves for them. We can pray and, in concrete ways, share our bread with a family in need.
exp.2:31:
Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion. The phrase "even if He causes grief" means "even if He causes grief," and the verse states it plainly as a real possibility. "Will show compassion" means that He will feel compassion and act with tenderness. Suffering is not God's final word.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. In the midst of the pain, in this chapter he remembers that God does not reject forever and that His loving devotion is great.

For today: if you are going through a painful season, do not interpret it as final abandonment. Speak to God honestly, remember His past mercies, and wait for His comfort, even if it takes a while to arrive.
exp.2:62:
He says the writer asks God to see everything his enemies do, from when they sit down to when they rise up, that is, at every moment of the day. He adds that they mock him in song, so that he has become the subject of their songs and jokes. The phrase "see how" here is a plea: "Look, Lord."

The one speaking is the writer of Lamentations, traditionally linked to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. In this chapter he speaks as someone who suffers, is mocked, and is persecuted, and he lays his case before God, trusting that He sees and hears.

For today: when someone mocks you or wounds you with words, you do not have to defend yourself alone or keep the pain inside. You can tell God honestly what you feel, trusting that He sees every detail and is a just judge.
exp.1:15:
Enemies of Jerusalem mock her after her fall. They open their mouths with contempt, hiss, and grind their teeth in rage. They say, "We have swallowed her up," and they celebrate that at last the day they had been waiting for has come.

The book of Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. The speaker describes the city's grief. Her enemies see her ruin as a victory, and the context says that God allowed this fall because of the people's sin.

For today: when someone falls or suffers, we should not rejoice in their pain. Instead, we should pray for that person, and if we ourselves are going through mockery or loss, we can bring our sorrow honestly before God.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that God, without showing pity, destroyed the homes and defenses of the people of Judah. The "dwellings of Jacob" are the people's homes, and the "fortified cities" are their walled towns. The phrase "defiled her kingdom and its princes" means that he stripped the kingdom and its rulers of their honor and dignity.

Lamentations is a song of grief, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. The speaker mourns the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC at the hands of Babylon. The poet sees it as God's judgment for the people's sin, and that is why he speaks with such raw honesty.

For today: we can be honest with God in our pain, without hiding what we feel. And when the consequences of our mistakes overtake us, this invites us to return to him with humility, remembering that later in the same book it speaks of his mercy that is renewed every morning.
exp.4:16:
It says the people are deeply sad. "Our hearts are faint" speaks of inner grief and exhaustion. "Our eyes grow dim" means the eyes have darkened: their light has faded, as when someone weeps so much or loses hope that they can no longer see clearly. "Because of this" and "because of these" point to everything before it: the lost joy, the mourning, and the fallen crown.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who after the destruction of Jerusalem acknowledge their sin and their suffering. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. What saddens them is seeing Zion desolate, the place of God's presence. But the book ends by recalling that God reigns forever.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can bring your honest sadness to God, acknowledge what you did wrong if needed, and remember that He remains on His throne even when your eyes are dim.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that the people now have to pay for basic things: water to drink and wood for the fire. "We must buy the water we drink" means they have to pay for it. Before, these were common and cheap things, and now they come at a price.

The speaker is the people of Judah, in a lament after the destruction of Jerusalem, probably by the Babylonians. They have lost their lands and their homes, and they live under foreigners who charge them even for what is most necessary. They grieve over the humiliation and the poverty. Many understand that the book was written by Jeremiah, but the text itself does not say so.

For today: when you go through scarcity or loss, you can bring your pain honestly before God, as this people does. Also remember to be thankful for the simple things you have today, like water and the warmth of home, and help those who cannot pay for them.
exp.2:46:
This verse says that the people lived in panic and fell into traps, like an animal caught. The word "pitfall" in the verse names a hidden hole or trap. "Devastation" means ruin, leaving the land laid waste. "Destruction" means collapse, something broken to pieces.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so openly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. He speaks on behalf of the people, who feel humbled before the nations, and his grief is so great that he goes on with rivers of tears.

For today: when you go through loss or fear, do not pretend you are fine. This Scripture shows that weeping and telling God honestly what hurts is a form of faith. Tell God your pain today, in your own words.
exp.2:10:
It says that God, seen as a hunter or an enemy, forced the author off his path, tore him to pieces, and left him without help. The phrase for "forced me off my path" means the path was bent away from its direction. The phrase for "tore me to pieces" means he was broken apart. The phrase for "left me without help" means he was left abandoned, ruined, and alone. It is very strong and painful language.

The speaker is a man grieving over the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, though the text does not say so directly. He feels that God has treated him the way a wild animal treats its prey. This is the honest complaint of someone in suffering, not a complete explanation of God. Later in this same chapter, the author recalls the faithfulness of the Lord.

When pain leaves you without strength, you can tell God honestly what you feel, without disguising it. The Bible makes room for complaint. And then, like the author, try to remember God's mercy, which remains there even when you cannot feel it.
exp.2:48:
My eyes overflow unceasingly, without relief. The verse describes tears that keep flowing and never stop, because there is no relief from the pain, no rest or comfort for his sorrow.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so explicitly. He weeps over the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. The verses that follow show that his weeping continues until God looks down and sees from heaven. His grief is also a way of waiting on God.

For today: when pain does not leave quickly, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can weep honestly before God and keep hoping that He sees you. You can also patiently accompany someone who is suffering, without rushing them to feel better.
exp.1:17:
The people cried out to God with broken hearts. Then the poet speaks to the wall of Jerusalem as if it were a person, asking it to let tears flow without stopping, like a river, day and night. Give yourself no relief, and let your eyes have no rest. The poet is urging the city to keep weeping and not to hold back its grief. The Hebrew of the first sentence is difficult, and some scholars read it differently.

Lamentations was written after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not name him. The author sees the people's pain, the mockery of their enemies, and the hunger of the children, and encourages the city to bring its sorrow to God.

Today we can speak with God honestly about what hurts us. Weeping before Him is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that He listens to us.
exp.2:51:
He says that his enemies hunted him relentlessly, the way one hunts a bird in order to catch it. "They hunted me" means they pursued him in order to capture him. The image of a bird being hunted matches the verse itself. "Without cause" means without reason, though he had done them no wrong.

Lamentations is a book of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. In this chapter, the speaker describes his suffering in a personal way. Some think he speaks on behalf of the whole people; others think it is the experience of one man. Both readings are possible. Even so, he cries out to God, hoping that he will look down from heaven.

When someone treats you unjustly, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can bring your complaint to God honestly, as this writer does. Praying sincerely helps you avoid repaying evil with evil and lets you hope that God sees and acts with justice.
exp.4:20:
What it says: The people ask God: "Restore us to yourself, and then we will return." The idea is that they cannot come back to God on their own; they ask Him to bring them back first. They also ask that God "renew" their days, that is, that He give them new life, as in the good times long ago, when they were close to Him.

Context: The people of Judah speak in Lamentations, after the destruction of Jerusalem. They are suffering and feel abandoned. First they remember that God reigns forever, and then they ask why He seems to have forgotten them. The following verse shows their fear: perhaps God has rejected them completely. Some readers see this ending as a prayer full of hope; others see a painful and uncertain conclusion.

For today: When you feel far from God or tired of your failures, do not wait until you have strength of your own. Pray sincerely: "Lord, restore me." He can give you the desire to return and renew your life.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that God has torn down his own dwelling place as easily as a flimsy shelter built among the plants in a garden. That dwelling place is the temple, the place where he met with his people. It also says that God has made Zion forget her appointed feasts and Sabbaths, and that in his fierce anger he has rejected both king and priest. "Appointed feasts" are the set religious festivals the people were to observe. "Despised" means rejected.

The speaker is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. He understands that ruin as the consequence of God's judgment on the people's disobedience.

Today, this text reminds us that no building or religious routine can replace a sincere relationship with God. We can draw near to Him with humility, and weep honestly when there is pain, trusting in his mercy.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that the people live pursued and worn out. "We are closely pursued" means that enemies or hardship keep chasing them, with no safe place to stop. They are weary from the constant work and strain, and they find no rest.

Lamentations is a poem of grief over the fall of Jerusalem, which tradition attributes to Jeremiah, although the book does not give his name. Here the people of Judah speak in their distress, after the destruction of the city. They live in poverty and subjection: they pay for water and firewood, and depend on other nations. The chapter ends with a prayer asking God to restore them.

When you are worn out and without rest, do not keep it silent: bring it to God honestly. This book teaches us that lamenting before Him is also a way of praying and of waiting for His help.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that the corrupt priests and prophets were treated as unclean people. The people shouted at them, "Go away! Unclean!" and "Away, away! Do not touch us!", as one would do with a leper or someone contaminated. "Go away" is the wording used in the verse, and "can stay here no longer" carries the sense of "cannot live there anymore." When they fled and wandered aimlessly, even the nations said, "They can stay here no longer."

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem. The spiritual leaders, who were meant to guide the people, were guilty of violence and injustice. That is why they became stained, discredited, and driven out.

For today: those who teach or lead others carry a great responsibility before God. Let us ask him for integrity, and examine our own lives with humility before pointing out the lives of others. God forgives those who repent with sincerity.
exp.1:12:
Here the writer speaks directly to Jerusalem, whom he addresses as "Daughter of Jerusalem" and "Virgin Daughter of Zion." He asks what he could say for her and what comparison he could make that would console her. He finds none, because her wound is as deep as the sea, vast and impossible to measure. He ends by asking who can ever heal her.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, whom tradition attributes to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so openly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its fall to Babylon. He has just described the hunger of the children in the streets. The verses that follow point out that the false prophets did not warn the people about their sin.

Today, when someone suffers a very great pain, there is no need to offer quick explanations. Sitting with them in tenderness and prayer means a great deal. And let us remember that only God can heal the deepest wounds.
exp.0:20:
Jerusalem cries out in pain, and no one comforts her. Her enemies heard of her misfortune and rejoiced, knowing that God caused it. She asks God to bring the day he announced, so that they will become like her in suffering.

Jerusalem speaks here, pictured as a widow left alone after Babylon destroyed the city. She acknowledges that her fall came because of her rebellion. Her plea for justice against her enemies is a cry of pain; many interpreters see in it the desire that God also judge those who were cruel to her.

When you feel alone and without comfort, do not hide your pain. Bring it to God honestly, even acknowledging your failures. He hears those who cry out, and you can leave justice in his hands rather than taking revenge.
exp.2:65:
You ask God to pursue your enemies in his anger and destroy them, so that they no longer exist under the heavens. "Pursue them" means to chase after them without rest. "Anger" is very strong wrath. "Destroy" means to exterminate them or bring them to ruin.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, wounded by the mockery and cruelty of his enemies. It is a prayer of grief that leaves justice in God's hands rather than in one's own. Scholars understand these prayers in different ways.

For today: when someone has hurt you, you can be honest with God about your pain and your anger. Entrust justice to him rather than taking revenge. Jesus also taught us to pray for those who mistreat us (Matthew 5:44).
exp.4:9:
The verse says the hunger was so intense and lasted so long that the people's skin felt hot and feverish, like the wall of an oven. The phrase "with fever from our hunger" describes the burning sensation that comes when the body has no food. The words "as hot as an oven" mean that their skin burned with heat.

The people of Judah speak in a lament prayer, after the fall of Jerusalem. Many understand it to be the time of the Babylonian invasion, though the text does not give every detail. The people tell God about their suffering: hunger, humiliation and fear. Lamentations 5 is a plea asking that God remember them and restore them.

When the pain is very great, there is no need to pretend to be strong. We can speak to God with sincerity, tell him everything and ask him for help. We can also remember those who go hungry today and help them with generosity.
exp.3:1:
This verse compares the people of Jerusalem to pure gold, something of great value. Now they are treated like ordinary clay jars, the kind a potter makes, which are common objects that break easily. The words "precious" and "esteemed" here describe how the sons of Zion were once worth their weight in gold, and how they are now regarded as things of little worth.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem, probably before the Babylonian army, around 586 BC. He describes the pain of a people who lost their dignity, their temple, and even their security.

For today: our worth does not depend on how we are treated or on our falls. When someone feels despised, they can remember that God sees them with compassion. And if we know someone who is wounded, let us treat them with dignity and help them.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that God's mercies, mentioned in the previous verse, are renewed every day, like a fresh gift at dawn. And it recognizes that God's faithfulness is great, meaning that he keeps his word and does not abandon his people. "They are new every morning" means "they are renewed every day"; "mercies" means his kindness and compassion.

The speaker is the author of the book, traditionally identified as Jeremiah, although the text itself does not give his name. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem, in the midst of great sorrow. Right in the middle of the weeping, he decides to remember who God is, and that brings back his hope. That is why he says: "I will wait."

For today: at the start of the day, before thinking about your problems, take a moment to thank God for one concrete sign of his care. Even if yesterday was hard, today you have his new mercy, enough for whatever you face.
exp.4:0:
This verse says the people are asking God to attend to their suffering. "Remember" does not mean that God has forgotten, but that they are pleading with him to act and to take notice of them. "Disgrace" means shame, mockery, or humiliation. "Look and see" is a sincere plea: "Lord, look at what we have become."

Lamentations 5 is a prayer of the community of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the text itself does not state this clearly. This chapter is the last one and begins with a group cry. The verses that follow describe losses: lands in the hands of strangers, broken families, and great need.

For today: when you are wounded or ashamed, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can speak with God with complete frankness and tell him what hurts. Praying honestly is an act of faith, because you trust that he listens.
exp.2:35:
Lamentations 3:36 says that twisting a person's case against them, that is, making someone lose their lawsuit through deceit or injustice, is something the Lord does not approve. The word used for "twisting" means to distort or ruin. Here three injustices are listed one after another: crushing prisoners, denying a person their rights, and subverting their case. The verse is often understood to mean that the Lord does not approve of such things. Some scholars also read a related idea as a question: does the Lord not see it?

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book itself does not say so. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and, in the middle of his grief, clings to hope in a just God who sees the suffering.

Today, if you see injustice at your work, in your family, or in your community, do not keep silent. God cares about those treated unjustly, and you can defend someone with truth and honesty.
exp.1:13:
It says that the prophets of Jerusalem announced false and worthless things to the people. The visions they described were empty and deceptive, with no truth or sense in them. They did not expose the people's guilt, which might have led them to change course and avoid captivity, the forced removal of people into a foreign land. Instead, the messages they gave were empty and misleading, pointing the people away from the right path.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its destruction by Babylon. Before the disaster, many prophets said that everything would be fine, and for that reason no one responded in time.

For today: let us look for voices that tell the truth with love, even when it hurts, and not only words that comfort us. Let us ask God for humility to hear correction and return to Him in time.
exp.2:45:
All their enemies open their mouths against us, speaking with scorn and attacking them with words. To open the mouth against someone can mean mocking them, speaking with contempt, or shouting with joy over their downfall. Here it is understood mainly as mockery and accusation.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not give his name. He weeps over the destruction of Jerusalem, probably by the Babylonians, around 586 B.C. The people feel that God is not hearing their prayer and that the nations around them rejoice in their ruin. It is a sincere lament, not an answer already resolved.

When you feel humiliated or criticized by others, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can bring your sadness to God honestly, as this writer does. Speaking to him frankly is a form of faith, and shortly after, this same chapter speaks of God's mercy that is renewed every morning.
exp.2:40:
This verse invites us to pray with our whole being. To lift up our hearts and hands to God means that the gesture of raising our hands should be joined to a sincere heart. The phrase "to God in heaven" points to the same truth: it is not enough to make an outward gesture, because God looks at the inside.

The one speaking is the author of the book, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the text does not say so explicitly. Jerusalem has been destroyed and the people are suffering. Instead of complaining, the author calls for examining one's own life and returning to God. The verses that follow admit the people's rebellion and express grief over the judgment they have received.

For today: when you are in difficulty, before you complain, pause. Be honest with God, acknowledge what you need to correct, and pray with an open heart, trusting that He listens.
exp.3:10:
God says he let his full anger fall on Jerusalem, and he compares it to a fire that was kindled in Zion and burned down to its very base. The phrase "has exhausted His wrath" means he carried his anger through to the end. The image of anger "poured out" is of wrath falling like hot liquid. The "foundations" are the base of the city.

Lamentations is a song of grief, and tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the book does not state this directly. The author mourns the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, around 586 BC. The verses that follow explain that it happened because of the sins of the people, of their prophets, and of their priests.

For today: God takes sin seriously, and we should hear this with humility. But this same book also speaks of his mercy, which is renewed every morning (3:22-23). We can return to him with sincerity and hope.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that God is righteous, and that Jerusalem admits she rebelled against his command. Then she calls on all people to listen and to look at her suffering, because her young men and young women have been taken away as prisoners. The young men and maidens are the two groups she names, and being carried off as prisoners to another land is what it means to go into captivity.

The one speaking is Jerusalem, pictured as a woman mourning after the destruction of the city, at the time of its fall to Babylon. The book is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the text itself does not give his name. She admits her guilt, but she also expresses her pain and her loneliness.

For today: we can be honest with God. Admitting our mistakes without excuses does not take away our right to grieve and to ask for comfort. We can say to him: "You are righteous, and I am wounded."
exp.4:10:
They abused the women in Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and the virgins in the towns of Judah. Here "abused" refers to sexual violence, and "virgins" refers to young women who had not yet married. No one was spared, either in the main city or in the countryside.

Lamentations is a song of grief over the fall of Jerusalem, which is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. The speaker describes the suffering of the people after the Babylonian conquest: hunger, fear, and humiliation. The verse is part of a list of horrors that the people present before God.

For today: God is not shocked when we speak to him frankly about pain. We can pray with honesty, without embellishment. Moreover, this text calls us to defend and accompany those who suffer abuse, listening to them with respect and without judgment.
exp.2:60:
This verse says that God has heard the insults of the enemies and all their plots against the speaker. The word for "insults" refers to shameful mockery meant to humiliate, and the plots are secret schemes to do harm. The speaker reminds God that none of it has escaped his notice.

The book of Lamentations is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so clearly. Here the speaker speaks as someone who suffers, surrounded by people who mock him and plan his ruin. At this point in the chapter, after much pain, he trusts that God sees his situation and can defend his cause.

When someone insults you or plots against you, you are not alone. You can tell God everything honestly, holding nothing back, and leave justice in his hands instead of taking revenge.
exp.0:10:
All her people groan as they search for bread. To get food, they have traded their treasures and valuable things, just to keep themselves alive. In the end, the city asks God to look at it, because it feels despised and humiliated.

Here Jerusalem speaks, personified as a woman who is suffering. After the invasion and the siege, there is hunger and poverty. The book understands this as a consequence of the people's sin, but it also lets us see real grief. According to tradition, Jeremiah wrote the book, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: when you are exhausted or in need, do not pretend to be strong. You can pray honestly, with a prayer like this: "Look, Lord, at how I am." God is not offended by your pain, and you can also ask for help from people you trust.
exp.2:20:
The writer chooses to call one specific thought to mind, or to "set again in his heart," and that is why he can keep on hoping.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem and the suffering of his people. Just before this, he sinks into his grief, but here he turns in a new direction. What he recalls comes in the verses that follow: the mercy and faithfulness of God, which never come to an end.

When pain overwhelms you, do not ignore what you feel, but also choose to remember who God is. You can write down three times when He helped you and go over them when distress comes. In this way your hope rests on His character, not on your circumstances.
exp.2:54:
This verse says the person called on God by name from a very deep and dark place. "To call upon" means to cry out to God or ask him for help. The "depths of the Pit" describes a place far down, dark and cut off, with no way out on one's own. God appears as the only one to turn to when everything seems lost.

The speaker in Lamentations is usually taken to be a poet mourning the fall of Jerusalem. Tradition attributes the book to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. In chapter 3 he speaks in the first person, perhaps for himself and also for all his people. He describes anguish: stones piled on him, waters covering him, a sense of death. Even so, he prays, and God answers him: "Fear not."

For today: when you feel trapped or without strength, do not wait until you have beautiful words. Cry out to God sincerely, from wherever you are. He hears even the deepest cry.
exp.3:16:
They say the people grew tired of looking and waiting for help that never came. "Worn out" means drained of strength. "Useless help" is help that accomplishes nothing. They hoped a nation nearby would save them, but those people had no power to do it.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who mourn the fall of Jerusalem. Many believe the book was written by Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. While the city was under siege, they looked to human allies, probably Egypt, instead of turning back to God. The verse shows the disappointment of someone who trusted in the wrong thing.

For today: think about what things you hope will rescue you, such as money, influence, or people. They can fail. Bring your burdens to God in prayer and trust in Him first, without despising the good help others may be able to give you.
exp.2:61:
This verse says that enemies speak against the one who is suffering, and that their slander and plots against him never stop all day long. "Slander and murmuring" refers to their words, what they whisper and say against him. "Assailants" are those who attack him.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. In chapter 3 he speaks of his personal pain, and at the same time he seems to voice the grief of his people after the fall of Jerusalem. Here he tells God how his assailants attack him with mockery and plots. The neighboring verses show that he trusts God sees everything and will do justice.

For today: when someone speaks badly of you or makes you feel persecuted, do not carry that distress alone. Tell God honestly what you hear and feel, and leave justice in his hands, without taking revenge.
exp.0:3:
The roads to Zion are in mourning, because no one comes to her appointed feasts anymore. The city's gates lie deserted, her priests groan in grief, her young women grieve, and the whole city is bitter with anguish. The feasts are the festivals God commanded his people to keep, and the roads are the paths that led to the city.

The book is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem, probably before Babylon, around 586 B.C. Tradition ascribes it to Jeremiah, though the text does not give his name. Here the poet speaks, describing the city as a wounded widow. The verses that follow explain that the people suffered because of their rebellions against God.

For today: when grief reaches you, do not hide it or pretend it away. This book teaches us to weep honestly before God. Bringing your sorrow to him in prayer is a step of faith, not of weakness.
exp.3:7:
This passage says that hunger has changed people who were once admired, so that their appearance is blacker than soot and no one recognizes them in the street. Their skin has shriveled on their bones and become as dry as a stick.

The author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly, speaks here. He weeps for Jerusalem after it was besieged and destroyed. The people described as having once been set apart and of noble appearance in the previous verse are now unrecognizable because of the siege. The poet shows the pain and the consequences of the people's sin.

Today we can look with compassion on those who suffer hunger or poverty, without judging them by their appearance. God draws near to the one who weeps, and we can help with something concrete: sharing food or supporting someone who needs it.
exp.2:41:
The verse says the people admit their guilt. "We have sinned and rebelled" means they rose up against God, and the BSB's "You have not forgiven" means that, at that moment, they feel God has not taken away the punishment.

The speaker is the prophet, probably Jeremiah according to tradition, together with the people of Judah. They mourn the destruction of Jerusalem. First there is an invitation to examine one's own life and return to God, and here they confess their sin. What follows shows their pain, because they feel God is distant and angry.

For today: before we complain to God about our suffering, we can be honest and confess our faults. Acknowledging the wrong is not the end, but the first step toward returning to Him, who promises to forgive the one who repents.
exp.3:21:
The verse says that Jerusalem, the daughter of Zion, has now paid in full for her wrongdoing, and that God will not let her be taken into exile again. Edom, however, will face God's judgment: he will punish Edom's wickedness and expose its sins. To be carried away means to be taken captive to another land, and iniquity means wrongdoing or guilt.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, a book that tradition ascribes to Jeremiah, though the book itself does not name him. He grieves over the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Edom, a neighboring nation, had celebrated that disaster. The poem closes with hope: Judah's suffering has a limit, and God also judges those who mock the pain of others. Some readers take the words "will not prolong your exile" to refer to that particular exile.

For today: when you go through a hard season, trust that God sets a limit to suffering and does not forget his own. And resist rejoicing at the misfortune of others; leave justice in God's hands.
exp.4:5:
The verse says the people "submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." In other words, they gave themselves over to these powerful nations, making agreements with them so that they would have food and would not go hungry.

The book of Lamentations is a lament over the fall of Jerusalem. It is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the text does not say so directly. Here the people speak, confessing their misery and their dependence on foreign powers. Some think Egypt and Assyria represent political alliances of the past; others, that they are symbolic names for any power that dominated them. There is no single interpretation that can be held with certainty.

For today: when we are in need, it is easy to trust anything that promises security. We can work and seek help wisely, but we should ask ourselves where our heart truly rests. God remains the one who sustains us.
exp.2:36:
This verse asks a question to make us think: who can speak and see something come to pass unless the Lord has ordained it? In other words, no one can bring about events that fall outside the Lord's control. Here "ordained" means decreed, or allowed to happen.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. In the midst of the pain, he remembers that God governs all things, even the injustice the people suffer. The verses that follow invite us to examine ourselves before complaining. Some understand that God directs events, and others that He permits them.

Today, when something hard comes into your life, do not stop at complaint. Pause, pray, and trust that God remains sovereign and wise. Examine your heart, ask Him for direction, and wait for His mercy.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the LORD carried out what he had planned long before. He brought down Jerusalem without showing pity, allowed its enemies to gloat over it, and raised up its foes in strength against it. The phrase "He has exalted the horn of your foes" means that he gave them power and victory, since a horn was a common picture of strength.

Here speaks the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns for Jerusalem after its fall to Babylon. He recognizes that this was not chance: the people had been warned by their prophets that turning away from God would bring judgment. The enemies mocked, but the grief sees the disaster in the light of God's word.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not hide your pain or blame others. Be honest before God, acknowledge whatever is true, and cry out to him, because he is also the God who lets himself be reached by tears.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the soul of the one speaking keeps returning to his suffering and cannot forget it. The reader sees "Surely my soul remembers," so the verse uses that wording: "remembers it again and again." "Humbled" here means brought low, sunk down by grief.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, although the book does not say so directly. He writes after the destruction of Jerusalem. At the darkest point of his complaint, he admits that his spirit has sunk low. But the next verse turns: as he remembers the mercy of God, he regains hope.

For today: you do not have to pretend that the pain does not exist. You can tell God honestly how you feel. And when sad memories surround you, try also to remember something of God's faithfulness in your life. In this way, your hope can rise little by little.
exp.2:39:
It says we should examine carefully how we have lived. "Examine" means to look into something closely and thoroughly, and "test" invites us to keep looking honestly at what we find. "Turn back to the LORD" means returning to God, that is, repenting and trusting Him again.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not state this explicitly. He mourns the destruction of Jerusalem. Instead of only complaining, he speaks as one of the people and joins them in acknowledging their guilt. The verses that follow show a prayer of confession.

For today: before we complain or blame others, let us take a quiet time to pray and ask God what we need to correct. Then, let us take a concrete step back toward Him.
exp.0:0:
It says that Jerusalem, once full of people and respected among the nations, is now lonely and empty. The writer compares her to a widow: without a husband, without protection, and without support. "Once so full of people" describes a city crowded with inhabitants. The verse also says she has become a slave, meaning she is now under the control of others, like a conquered people. She who once held authority over other regions is now dominated.

The book is a lament over the destruction of Jerusalem, probably when Babylon conquered her in 586 B.C. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, but the text does not name its author. The one speaking weeps with grief for his city and acknowledges that her fall was the consequence of the people's disobedience.

For today: God allows us to weep honestly. When you feel loss or loneliness, do not hide it; bring it to God in prayer, for He hears honest lament.
exp.2:58:
The speaker asks God to look at the wrong he is suffering and to take up his defense. "Wrong done to me" means an offense or unfair treatment. "Vindicate my cause" is like asking someone to stand up in court and prove that you are in the right. It is a prayer of trust: you have already seen it, Lord; now act.

The one speaking in Lamentations is a poet who grieves over the destruction of Jerusalem and the mockery of its enemies. He is traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so clearly. In this passage he recalls that God had heard and rescued him before, and that is why he dares to ask for help again.

When someone treats you unjustly, you do not have to take revenge or prove that you are right at all costs. Tell God honestly what happened, remember how he helped you before, and leave your case in his hands.
exp.1:19:
What it says: Jerusalem asks God to look at her suffering and to consider whom He has ever treated like this. She asks whether it is right that women should eat their own offspring, the infants they once nursed, and whether priests and prophets should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord. In the verse, "look" means "look closely," and the "infants" are the young children the mothers had cared for.

Context: The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so clearly. He speaks after Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon, around 586 BC. There was hunger and death, and the writer dares to bring his complaint before God with tears, hiding nothing.

For today: When pain overwhelms you, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God with complete honesty what you feel, even with hard questions. Honest prayer is also faith, because you keep coming to Him.
exp.0:16:
Zion, that is, Jerusalem, stretches out her hands asking for help, but no one comforts her. Stretching out the hands is a gesture of pleading or pain. According to the text, the Lord decreed that her neighbors would become her enemies, surrounding Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them, something they regard as repulsive and despise.

Lamentations is a poem of mourning over the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 B.C. Here the city speaks as a personified figure, while the author, whom tradition often identifies with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so, describes her grief. The verse acknowledges that this disaster was not chance but a consequence of God's judgment, as the following verse confirms: "The LORD is righteous."

Today, when you feel lonely or suffer the consequences of your mistakes, you can be honest before God, acknowledge your failure, and cry out to Him. He is the one who truly comforts.
exp.2:42:
It says God showed his anger with force. "You have covered Yourself in anger" is like spreading a net or a curtain: his anger fell on the people. "You pursued us" speaks of a discipline they felt was relentless. "You have killed without pity" describes the harshness of the punishment, with no visible relief.

The speaker is the author of Lamentations, traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem. In the verses before, the people acknowledge their rebellion. Now he describes with pain what they lived through as God's judgment. It is an honest prayer, made out of suffering.

For today: when you go through pain or the consequences of your mistakes, you can speak to God with sincerity, without pretending. Acknowledge your fault, express your pain, and keep drawing near to Him. Later in this same book, it speaks of his mercy being renewed every morning.
exp.1:20:
Lamentations 2:21 describes young and old lying together on the ground in the streets of Jerusalem. The young men and young women have fallen by the sword. The poet says that God himself has slain them in the day of his anger, and that he has slaughtered them without compassion. The poet feels that God allowed this punishment as an expression of his anger.

The one speaking is the author of Lamentations, traditionally identified with Jeremiah, although the book does not state this clearly. He mourns the fall of Jerusalem, probably in the year 586 BC, when the Babylonians destroyed it. He understands it as God's judgment for the people's sin, but he expresses it with grief and does not hide his anguish.

For today: when the pain overwhelms you, you can bring it to God with complete honesty. He is not frightened by your tears or your questions. Praying honestly is also an act of faith.
exp.3:12:
This verse explains why Jerusalem fell: the blame rests on its spiritual leaders. The prophets and priests, who were meant to guide the people in truth and justice, failed badly. The phrase "who shed the blood of the righteous" means that they caused the death of innocent people, or allowed it to happen.

Lamentations is a song of mourning, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, though the book does not say so directly. The author grieves the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. Here he recognizes that the disaster was no accident: corrupt leaders bore a heavy responsibility. The verses that follow show them wandering like blind people, stained with blood.

Those who teach or lead others carry a greater responsibility. Today we can pray for our pastors and leaders, and honestly examine how we use any influence we have, so that it is exercised with integrity and not with selfishness.
exp.2:24:
God is good to those who trust in him and wait for him, that is, to the one who seeks him with all their heart. The word "LORD" here is the name of God as it appears in the verse. "Wait" here does not only mean enduring the passing of time, but trusting with patience. "Soul" refers to the whole person, with their desires and their inner life. "Seeks" means to look for him earnestly.

Lamentations expresses grief over the destruction of Jerusalem, and tradition usually attributes it to Jeremiah, although the book does not say so openly. The speaker comes out of deep suffering, but in the middle of it recalls that God is faithful and that his mercies are renewed every morning. He says, "The LORD is my portion," and for that reason he decides to wait.

Today, when a hard situation drags on, you can begin the day praying simply: "Lord, you are my portion; today I seek you and trust in you." Waiting on God is not becoming passive, but moving forward with faith and patience.
exp.1:3:
This verse describes God as a warrior who prepares to fight against his own people. The first image is of him bending his bow like an enemy, ready to shoot. The verse speaks of him killing all who were pleasing to the eye, which refers to what was most dear and precious in Jerusalem. The words "the tent of the Daughter of Zion" are a poetic way of speaking of the city and its homes. His wrath was poured out like fire.

Lamentations is a song of mourning, and tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, although the text does not give his name. The author mourns the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, in the year 586 BC. He understands that ruin as the consequence of the people's sin, and so he speaks with pain and raw honesty.

For today: when we go through losses or discipline, we can weep sincerely before God, without disguising the pain. And since the book moves forward, we can also hope in his mercy.
exp.4:7:
It says that people who were once of the lower class, such as servants or slaves, now rule over God's people. The verse itself makes clear that these rulers were once beneath them, so the wording here follows the verse directly. And no one could rescue them from their hands.

The speaker is the people of Judah, who mourn after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon. The rulers may be officials of the conquerors or people of little authority who now govern. Scholars understand this in several ways. The people recognize that they suffer for their own sin and that of their fathers, and they feel that they have no help.

For today: when you feel trapped or without a way out, be honest with God in prayer, as this people was. Do not hide your pain. Lamentations teaches that one can grieve and still return to God, hoping for his mercy.
exp.1:10:
The speaker is broken by grief. His eyes are worn out from weeping, and his insides are churning. He says his heart has been poured out, which is his way of saying his heart feels shattered. "The daughter of my people" refers to Jerusalem and its people. The hardest thing he sees is children and infants fainting from hunger in the streets of the city.

This is the book of Lamentations, written after Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Tradition attributes it to Jeremiah, though the text itself does not give a name. The one speaking does not watch from a distance; he suffers alongside his people. The verses that follow show children asking their mothers for bread.

For today: do not rush to explain away or fix someone else's pain. Learn to weep with those who weep, staying close and praying with them. God does not ask us to pretend to be strong; the Bible itself makes room for tears.

sum.2: In this chapter, the author describes his pain and suffering with grief, as if God himself had surrounded him and wounded him. But in the middle of his distress, he remembers that God's mercy and faithfulness are new every morning, and so he decides to wait for Him. He invites the people to turn back to God, and at the end he cries out for help and justice.
sum.1: Lamentations 2 describes, with deep grief, how God, in his anger, allowed Jerusalem to be destroyed. Its walls, its temple, and its leaders all fell, and the false prophets did not warn the city of its sin. The author mourns the hunger of the children and calls the people to cry out to God. The chapter ends with an anguished prayer asking God to look upon their suffering.
sum.4: In this chapter the people ask God to remember their shame and suffering. They have lost their homes, they go hungry, and they live under oppression. They acknowledge that they have sinned and that they are suffering because of it. Even so, they trust that God reigns forever, and they ask him to bring them back to himself and renew their days.
sum.0: Jerusalem, once great and full of people, is left alone and weeping, like a widow, after being defeated and taken into captivity. The text acknowledges that this came because of her sins and that God is just, yet the people suffer without comfort and ask God to look at their pain. They also pray that their enemies will receive punishment.
sum.3: Lamentations 4 describes with grief the fall of Jerusalem: the famine, the ruin, and the shame of the people, whose sins, especially those of prophets and priests, brought God's judgment. In the end, the punishment of Zion comes to an end, but Edom will be judged.
